The TARDBP gene encodes TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), which plays a critical role in RNA processing and DNA repair. Pathogenic variants in TARDBP are strongly associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a neurodegenerative disease characterized by motor neuron death. Mutations in TARDBP can lead to mislocalization and aggregation of TDP-43, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. This pathway includes mitochondrial complex I (CxI) genes, suggesting a link between TDP-43 dysfunction and mitochondrial impairment, which may exacerbate ALS pathology.  

\boxed{Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)}

The VHL allele is part of a genomic pathway regulating hypoxia-response genes. VHL, along with RBX1, ELOC, ELOB, and CUL2, forms an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that targets HIF1A for degradation under normoxic conditions. When VHL is dysfunctional, HIF1A accumulates, stabilizing the HIF1A-ARNT complex, which activates downstream genes like VEGFA, PDGFB, TGFA, and TGFB. This leads to increased angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and survival—hallmarks of tumor growth. This pathway is critically involved in the development of **von Hippel-Lindau disease**, a hereditary cancer syndrome characterized by hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and pheochromocytomas.  
\boxed{von Hippel-Lindau disease}

The CDKN2A allele encodes p16INK4a, a key inhibitor of CDK4/6, which regulates the G1/S transition in the cell cycle. Inactivation or mutation of CDKN2A disrupts this regulation, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation. This pathway involves TP53, which, when functional, activates CDKN1A (p21) to halt the cell cycle. However, MDM2 can inactivate TP53, reducing its tumor-suppressive effect. Deregulation of this network—through CDKN2A loss, TP53 mutation, or MDM2 overexpression—can lead to unchecked cell cycle progression, driven by E2F and cyclin-CDK complexes. This contributes to the development of melanoma and other cancers. 

\boxed{Melanoma}

The APP allele is associated with Alzheimer’s disease. The pathway begins with APP, which is cleaved to produce amyloid beta (Aβ), a key contributor to amyloid plaque formation in Alzheimer’s. Aβ activates muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChR), leading to downstream signaling through GNAQ, PLCB, IP3, and ITPR, which release Ca²⁺. Excess Ca²⁺ is transported into mitochondria via MCU, potentially triggering mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) opening and cytochrome c (CYCS) release, promoting apoptosis. These events are linked to neuronal dysfunction and death in Alzheimer’s disease.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The KCNC3 gene encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel involved in neuronal excitability. Mutations in KCNC3 are associated with **febrile seizures plus (FEPS+)**, a severe epilepsy syndrome characterized by fever-induced seizures and additional neurologic abnormalities. This allele contributes to impaired neuronal function, leading to heightened seizure susceptibility.  
\boxed{Febrile seizures plus}

The APP allele contributes to **Alzheimer's disease**. The pathway outlines a sequence beginning with the amyloid beta precursor protein (APP), leading to the production of Abeta, which is a key pathological component in Alzheimer's. This triggers a cascade involving muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChR), GNAQ, PLCB, IP3, ITPR, and calcium signaling, ultimately affecting mitochondrial function through MCU and MPTP, leading to cytochrome c release (CYCS). These events are implicated in neuronal dysfunction and cell death characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The ATXN3 allele contributes to **Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3 (SCA3)**, also known as Machado-Joseph disease. This neurodegenerative disorder is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the ATXN3 gene, leading to the production of a toxic, expanded polyglutamine protein. This mutant protein aggregates in neurons, particularly in the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord, causing progressive degeneration of motor neurons. The pathway described involves calcium dysregulation, which is implicated in neuronal dysfunction and death. ATXN3's role in this pathway, especially through its interaction with ITPR1 and calcium signaling, may exacerbate mitochondrial dysfunction and apoptosis, contributing to the pathogenesis of SCA3.

\boxed{Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3}

The SOD1 allele is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). This pathway involves oxidative stress (SOD1), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (BIP, HSPA5), and the PERK signaling cascade (EIF2AK3, EIF2S1, ATF4, DDIT3), which are all key in ALS pathogenesis. Mutations in SOD1 lead to misfolding and aggregation, inducing ER stress and neurodegeneration.  
\boxed{Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)}

The APP (amyloid beta precursor protein) allele is central to the amyloid pathway, leading to the production of Abeta peptides. Accumulation of Abeta is a key factor in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer's disease. The network includes proteasome subunits (20S and 26S), which are involved in protein degradation. Dysfunction in this pathway may impair Abeta clearance, contributing to its accumulation and subsequent neurodegeneration.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The FGFR3 allele in this pathway contributes to **achondroplasia**, a common form of dwarfism. FGFR3 is a receptor tyrosine kinase that, when activated, initiates a signaling cascade involving GRB2, SOS, RAS, RAF, MEK, ERK, MSK1, and MYC. This pathway is critical for regulating cell proliferation and differentiation, particularly in chondrocytes during bone development. Mutations in FGFR3 lead to constitutive activation of the pathway, resulting in excessive signaling that impairs normal skeletal growth. This over-activation causes the characteristic short-limbed dwarfism seen in achondroplasia.  
\boxed{achondroplasia}

The HTT allele encodes the huntingtin protein, which is central to the pathology of **Huntington's disease**. In this pathway, HTT interacts with STX1A and regulates VGCC(N-type) channels, influencing intracellular Ca²⁺ levels. Mutations in HTT, particularly CAG trinucleotide repeat expansions, lead to abnormal huntingtin protein accumulation, disrupting neuronal function and causing progressive neurodegeneration. This contributes to the development of **Huntington's disease**, a fatal, inherited neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms.  
\boxed{Huntington's disease}

The PRKN gene encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Mutations in PRKN are a major cause of recessive Parkinson's disease. This pathway, involving PRKN and ubiquitin conjugating enzymes like UBE2L3 and UBE2L6, likely contributes to the degradation of damaged proteins. Dysfunction in this pathway can lead to impaired protein quality control and mitochondrial dysfunction, which are hallmarks of Parkinson's disease. Thus, the PRKN allele contributes to **Parkinson's disease**.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

AXIN1 is a key negative regulator in the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway. Mutations in AXIN1 disrupt its ability to inhibit β-catenin (CTNNB1), leading to its accumulation and activation of TCF/LEF transcription factors, which in turn upregulate target genes like MYC and CCND1. This unchecked signaling contributes to uncontrolled cell proliferation, a hallmark of cancer. Specifically, AXIN1 mutations are implicated in colorectal cancer, where they compromise the tumor suppressive function of the WNT pathway.  
\boxed{Colorectal cancer}

The AR allele in this pathway is involved in androgen signaling, modulating the expression of KLK3, which is linked to prostate-specific antigen (PSA) production. This pathway is central to prostate biology. Dysregulation of AR activity is strongly associated with **prostate cancer**, as it drives cell proliferation and tumor progression. Mutations or hyperactivation of AR can lead to uncontrolled growth of prostate cells.  
\boxed{Prostate Cancer}

The PSEN1 gene is central to the amyloidogenic pathway, contributing to the production of amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptides. Mutations in PSEN1 are strongly associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). The provided pathway illustrates how PSEN1 initiates a cascade involving calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptosis, which are key features of AD pathogenesis. PSEN1* likely denotes a disease-associated variant that disrupts normal function, leading to neurodegeneration. This pathway links PSEN1 to mitochondrial calcium overload, MPTP opening, and cytochrome c release, all contributing to neuronal death. Thus, the biological effect of this PSEN1 allele is to increase the risk of Alzheimer's disease.

\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The SPTBN2 allele is involved in a genomic pathway that modulates intracellular calcium signaling through the GRM1-GNAQ-PLCB-IP3-ITPR-Ca²⁺ cascade. Dysregulation of this pathway may disrupt calcium homeostasis, affecting neuronal function and axonal integrity. This contributes to **hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP)**, a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive lower limb spasticity. SPTBN2 encodes a spectrin protein essential for axonal stability, and mutations in this gene disrupt the structural and functional integrity of neurons, particularly in the central nervous system. Thus, the SPTBN2 allele is implicated in hereditary spastic paraplegia.  
\boxed{hereditary spastic paraplegia}

The CACNA1A gene encodes a subunit of the voltage-gated calcium channel, which plays a critical role in neuronal excitability and signaling. Mutations in CACNA1A are strongly associated with familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM), a rare, severe form of migraine with transient motor deficits. These mutations lead to altered calcium influx, disrupting normal neuronal function and contributing to the pathophysiology of the disease. Additionally, CACNA1A mutations have been implicated in ataxia and other neurologic disorders.  
\boxed{Familial hemiplegic migraine}

The PSAP gene encodes prosaposin, a precursor to saposins, which are essential for the activity of lysosomal enzymes like GBA and GALC. Mutations in PSAP lead to a deficiency in saposins, impairing the function of these enzymes. This deficiency results in the accumulation of glycosphingolipids in lysosomes, causing cellular damage. This contributes to **Saposin Deficiency**, a rare lysosomal storage disorder. Specifically, PSAP mutations are associated with **Krabbe Disease**, a severe neurodegenerative disorder.  
\boxed{Krabbe Disease}

The ATXN3 allele is associated with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also known as Machado-Joseph disease. This neurodegenerative disorder results from expansions of CAG trinucleotide repeats in the ATXN3 gene, leading to toxic accumulation of mutant ataxin-3 protein. The pathway involving ATXN3 interacts with autophagy-related genes (BECN1, PIK3C3, ATG14, PIK3R4, AMBRA1), highlighting its role in autophagy regulation. Dysfunctional autophagy may exacerbate neuronal dysfunction and cell death, contributing to the progressive degeneration observed in SCA3.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3}

The PRNP allele is implicated in prion disease, a group of progressive neurodegenerative disorders. The pathway highlights the involvement of PRNP (prion protein) in a signaling cascade leading to ROS (reactive oxygen species) production via NOX2. This suggests a role for oxidative stress in disease pathology. Mutations in PRNP, such as those causing misfolding of the prion protein, are directly linked to conditions like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), including sporadic, familial, and variant forms. The pathway underscores the molecular mechanisms involving signaling through CAV, FYN, PI3K, PRKCD, and NOX2, which may contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration.  

\boxed{Prion disease}

The NRAS allele, when mutated, can constitutively activate the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway by promoting the conversion of PIP2 to PIP3, leading to AKT activation. This results in uncontrolled cell proliferation and survival, contributing to tumorigenesis. Specifically, NRAS mutations are commonly associated with melanoma, a type of skin cancer, and certain hematologic malignancies. These mutations are oncogenic drivers in these diseases.  
\boxed{Melanoma}

The ATXN3 gene is associated with **Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3 (SCA3)**, also known as **Machado-Joseph Disease**. This neurodegenerative disorder is caused by expanded CAG repeats in the ATXN3 gene, leading to the production of a toxic protein that disrupts neuronal function, particularly in the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord. The pathway described includes calcium signaling components like ITPR1 and MCU, which are critical for cellular homeostasis. Dysfunctional ATXN3 may impair calcium regulation, contributing to neuronal degeneration. Thus, the ATXN3 allele contributes to **Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3**.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3}

The PTEN gene acts as a tumor suppressor by dephosphorylating PIP3, thereby inhibiting the AKT signaling pathway. Mutations in PTEN that reduce its function lead to constitutive activation of AKT, promoting cell survival, growth, and proliferation. This dysregulation contributes to uncontrolled cell division and tumor formation. PTEN mutations are associated with several cancers, including glioblastoma, endometrial carcinoma, and breast cancer, as well as genetic syndromes like Cowden syndrome. The biological effect of a PTEN allele with reduced function is increased cancer risk.

\boxed{Cancer}

The ATXN3 allele is implicated in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), a neurodegenerative disorder. ATXN3 is part of a pathway involving autophagy-related genes (BECN1, PIK3C3, ATG14, PIK3R4, AMBRA1), which regulate cellular degradation processes. Mutations in ATXN3 lead to protein misfolding and aggregation, disrupting autophagy and contributing to neuronal dysfunction. This pathway is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, and its dysfunction is linked to progressive neurodegeneration.  

\boxed{Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3}

The PSEN1 allele is associated with Alzheimer's disease. It is a key gene in the amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing pathway, contributing to the production of amyloid-beta peptides, which form plaques in the brains of Alzheimer's patients. The given pathway involves endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress signaling, with PSEN1 potentially influencing this pathway, linking it to neurodegenerative processes. This reinforces its role in Alzheimer's pathogenesis.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The PSEN1 gene encodes presenilin 1, a key component of the gamma-secretase complex involved in amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing. Mutations in PSEN1 are strongly associated with early-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). In the given pathway, PSEN1 activates ERN1, which in turn phosphorylates XBP1, a transcription factor involved in the unfolded protein response (UPR). Dysregulation of this pathway may contribute to ER stress and neurodegeneration. Therefore, PSEN1 mutations contribute to $\boxed{\text{Alzheimer's disease}}$.

The SQSTM1 allele contributes to **Neurodegenerative diseases**, specifically **Parkinson’s disease**. SQSTM1, also known as sequestosome 1, is involved in autophagy and protein degradation. Its dysregulation, often seen in mutations or altered expression, leads to impaired clearance of damaged proteins and mitochondria. This pathway—PINK1 → PRKN → SQSTM1 → LC3—is critical for mitophagy, the selective autophagy of damaged mitochondria. Mutations in SQSTM1 can disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of deleterious proteins and mitochondrial dysfunction, hallmark features of Parkinson’s disease.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The NRAS allele, when mutated, activates the RAS-PI3K-AKT signaling pathway, promoting cell survival and proliferation. This pathway is frequently dysregulated in cancer. Specifically, NRAS mutations are implicated in various malignancies, including melanoma, thyroid cancer, and leukemia. The activation of AKT leads to inactivation of BAD, preventing apoptosis. Thus, the biological effect of this NRAS allele is to contribute to tumorigenesis.  
\boxed{Cancer}

The VHL allele is part of a signaling pathway that regulates hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) activity. Under normal conditions, the VHL complex targets HIF-α for degradation. In VHL dysfunction, HIF-α accumulates, leading to the activation of downstream genes like VEGFA, CXCL8, and EPO, which promote angiogenesis, inflammation, and erythropoiesis. This contributes to tumor growth and vascular remodeling. The pathway's activation is linked to **clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC)**, a common kidney cancer.  
\boxed{Clear cell renal cell carcinoma}

The PRKN gene encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in mitochondrial quality control. Mutations in PRKN are a major cause of early-onset autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease. Parkin dysfunction leads to impaired mitophagy, resulting in the accumulation of damaged mitochondria and subsequent neuronal degeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. The pathway involving PRKN and MFN1/2 (mitofusins) is critical for mitochondrial dynamics and function. Disruption of this pathway contributes to neurodegeneration.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The CDK4 allele, when overactive, promotes uncontrolled cell cycle progression by phosphorylating RB1, leading to the release of E2F transcription factors. This activates genes required for DNA replication and cell division. Dysregulation of this pathway is a key feature in several cancers, particularly those involving the cell cycle checkpoint. The most direct and well-documented disease associated with CDK4 overactivity is **melanoma**. 

\boxed{melanoma}

The NRAS allele, when mutated, activates the RAS-PI3K-AKT signaling pathway by promoting continuous GTP binding, leading to sustained PI3K activity. This results in increased PIP3 production, which activates AKT. AKT then phosphorylates and inactivates BAD, a pro-apoptotic protein, thereby promoting cell survival and proliferation. This constitutive activation contributes to uncontrolled cell growth and is a common driver in various cancers.  

\boxed{Cancer}

The PSAP gene encodes prosaposin, a precursor to saposins, which are essential for the enzymatic activity of lysosomal enzymes like GBA and GALC. Mutations in PSAP lead to a deficiency in saposins, impairing the function of these enzymes. This results in the accumulation of undegraded substrates, primarily in lysosomes, leading to neurodegeneration. The condition is known as **Saposin Deficiency** or **Sphingolipidosis**, specifically **Krabbe disease** when related to GALC dysfunction. However, PSAP mutations are most directly linked to **Farber disease** (Farber lipogranulomatosis), a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder.  
\boxed{Farber disease}

The MET allele activates the MET receptor tyrosine kinase, initiating a signaling cascade involving GAB1, PI3K (via PIK3CA, PIK3CB, or PIK3CD), PIP3, and AKT, which phosphorylates BAD, promoting cell survival and growth. Dysregulation of this pathway is implicated in cancer, particularly in tumor growth, invasion, and resistance to therapy. This contributes to **malignant tumor progression**, specifically in cancers like **non-small cell lung cancer**, **gastric cancer**, and **hepatocellular carcinoma**.  
\boxed{Cancer}

The ABL1 allele, as part of the BCR-ABL fusion in this pathway, drives chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). BCR-ABL activates downstream effectors like PI3K, leading to AKT phosphorylation and survival signaling, while inhibiting BAD-mediated apoptosis. This results in uncontrolled cell proliferation and resistance to programmed cell death, hallmark features of CML. $\boxed{\text{Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)}}$

The PRKN allele, encoding parkin, is a key component of a signaling pathway involving PLCG1, IP3, and ITPR, which regulates intracellular calcium levels. Mutations in PRKN are strongly associated with autosomal recessive juvenile parkinsonism (ARJP), also known as Parkinson disease type 1 (PARK1). This disease is characterized by early-onset motor dysfunction due to dopaminergic neuron degeneration in the substantia nigra. The pathway likely contributes to neurodegeneration by disrupting calcium homeostasis, a critical factor in neuronal survival.  
\boxed{Parkinson disease}

The PRNP gene encodes the prion protein, and specific alleles of this gene, such as those with mutations, are associated with prion diseases. These neurodegenerative disorders involve the misfolding of the prion protein into a pathogenic form, leading to progressive brain damage. The NOTCH1 gene is involved in cell signaling and development, but its role in prion disease is less direct. The pathway PRNP* -> NOTCH1 may suggest a signaling interaction, though the primary disease linked to PRNP alleles is prion disease.  
\boxed{Prion disease}

The VHL allele is part of a signaling pathway that regulates hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) through the VHL-Elongin-CUL2 complex, which targets HIF for degradation. When VHL is dysfunctional, HIF accumulates, leading to the activation of downstream genes like VEGFA, CXCL8, SLC2A1 (GLUT1), and EPO. This results in increased vascularization and erythropoiesis. This pathway is dysregulated in Von Hippel-Lindau disease, a hereditary cancer syndrome characterized by the development of benign and malignant tumors in various organs. 

\boxed{Von Hippel-Lindau disease}

The HTT allele, associated with Huntington's disease, leads to the production of a mutant huntingtin protein. This mutant protein causes toxic accumulation, impaired intracellular signaling, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Specifically, the pathway involves NMDAR-mediated calcium influx, mitochondrial calcium overload via MCU, and subsequent mitochondrial permeability transition (MPTP), leading to cytochrome c release and activation of the apoptotic cascade (CASP9 → CASP3). This results in neuronal degeneration, particularly in the striatum and cortex. The disease is characterized by motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms.  
\boxed{Huntington's disease}

The KCNC3 gene encodes a voltage-gated potassium channel involved in regulating neuronal excitability. Mutations in KCNC3 are associated with **epilepsy**, specifically **autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy (ADNFLE)**. This condition is characterized by episodes of seizures originating from the frontal lobes, typically occurring during sleep. The KCNC3 allele contributes to disease by altering potassium channel function, leading to hyperexcitability in neurons and abnormal electrical activity in the brain. These genetic changes disrupt normal neuronal signaling, predisposing individuals to focal seizures.  
\boxed{Autosomal Dominant Nocturnal Frontal Lobe Epilepsy}

The PRKN allele encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Mutations in PRKN are a major cause of autosomal recessive juvenile Parkinson's disease (PD). Parkin plays a role in mitochondrial quality control and apoptosis. Its dysfunction leads to neuronal degeneration, primarily in dopaminergic neurons, contributing to the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The PRNP allele is associated with prion disease, a group of transmissible neurodegenerative disorders. In this pathway, PRNP interacts with BIP (a chaperone protein) and activates EIF2AK3, leading to a cascade involving EIF2S1, ATF4, and finally DDIT3. This pathway is involved in the unfolded protein response (UPR), which is triggered by misfolded proteins, such as those associated with prion disease. The biological effect of the PRNP allele is the initiation and progression of prion-related neurodegeneration, contributing to diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.  
\boxed{Prion disease}

The CACNA1A gene encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel subunit crucial for calcium influx in neurons. Mutations in CACNA1A are linked to impaired calcium signaling, leading to neuronal dysfunction. This contributes to **spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1)**, a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive loss of coordination and motor control. The allele disrupts normal channel function, causing abnormal neuronal firing and degeneration in the cerebellum and brainstem.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar ataxia type 1}

The TBK1 allele is involved in the autophagy pathway, specifically in the regulation of LC3-II through interactions with proteins like SQSTM1, OPTN, NDP52, TAX1BP1, and NBR1. Dysregulation of this pathway can impair autophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles. This contributes to neurodegenerative diseases, particularly amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). TBK1 mutations have been implicated in both familial and sporadic forms of ALS, affecting motor neuron survival and function. 

\boxed{Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)}

The SNCA gene encodes alpha-synuclein, a protein involved in synaptic function and membrane regulation. The SNCA allele in the provided pathway is linked to complex I (CxI) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, suggesting a role in mitochondrial dysfunction. Mutations in SNCA are strongly associated with Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and bradycinesia. Accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein leads to Lewy bodies, a hallmark of PD. This pathway's connection to complex I implies that SNCA may influence mitochondrial activity, contributing to neuronal stress and degeneration. Thus, the SNCA allele contributes to $\boxed{\text{Parkinson's disease}}$.

The PARK7 gene encodes DJ1, a protein involved in protecting neurons from oxidative stress. In the provided pathway, DJ1 interacts with DAXX and ASK1 to regulate JNK activation, which is linked to stress responses and apoptosis. Mutations in PARK7 are associated with early-onset Parkinson's disease. This allele contributes to neurodegenerative processes, impairing cellular protection mechanisms and leading to dopaminergic neuron loss.  

\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The BRAF allele, specifically the mutated form (e.g., V600E), activates the MAPK/ERK pathway by constitutively phosphorylating MEK, leading to persistent ERK activation. This uncontrolled signaling promotes cell proliferation and survival, contributing to tumorigenesis. This pathway abnormality is commonly observed in cancers such as melanoma, thyroid cancer, and colorectal cancer.  

\boxed{Melanoma}

The APRT gene encodes adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, an enzyme involved in purine salvage pathways. A deficiency or mutation in APRT leads to the accumulation of 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which can form kidney stones. This condition is known as **adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency**, also referred to as **2,8-dihydroxyadenine urolithiasis** or **APRT deficiency**. It is a rare inherited disorder typically presenting with recurrent kidney stones, hematuria, and flank pain. The biological effect of a pathogenic APRT allele is impaired purine metabolism, resulting in nephrolithiasis and potential renal failure if untreated.  
\boxed{Adenine Phosphoribosyltransferase Deficiency}

The RB1 gene encodes a tumor suppressor protein that regulates the cell cycle by inhibiting E2F transcription factors. Mutations or deletions in RB1 lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation, contributing to the development of retinoblastoma, a malignant tumor of the retina. The pathway RB1* // E2F highlights the interaction between RB1 and E2F proteins, which are crucial for cell cycle progression. Loss of functional RB1 allows E2F proteins to activate genes required for DNA replication, promoting unrestrained cell division. This genomic pathway dysfunction is a hallmark of retinoblastoma.

\boxed{Retinoblastoma}

The ATXN3 gene encodes ataxin-3, which is involved in the glutamate-mediated calcium signaling pathway. Mutations in ATXN3, particularly expansions of a polyglutamine tract, lead to toxic protein aggregation and dysfunction in motor and cognitive systems. This contributes to the neurodegenerative disease **Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3 (SCA3)**, also known as Machado-Joseph disease. The pathway shows how ATXN3 interacts with ITPR1 and IP3, modulating calcium release and mitochondrial function, which, when dysregulated, may exacerbate neuronal degeneration.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 3}

The SOD1 allele in this genomic pathway is linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1) is a key player in the pathway involving BIP, ATF6, and DDIT3, which are involved in the unfolded protein response (UPR) and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. Mutations in SOD1 contribute to ER stress and subsequent neurodegeneration, a hallmark of ALS. This pathway highlights the connection between oxidative stress, protein misfolding, and the progression of ALS.  
\boxed{Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)}

In the given pathway, PTEN* (a mutated or dysfunctional allele) leads to reduced PIP3 dephosphorylation, resulting in increased AKT activation. Hyperactivation of AKT promotes cell survival, growth, and proliferation, contributing to uncontrolled cell division. This dysregulation is frequently observed in various cancers, particularly in conditions such as **Cowden syndrome** and **breast, endometrial, and thyroid cancers**. The loss of PTEN function is a well-documented driver in these malignancies.

\boxed{Cowden syndrome}

The TP53 gene, a tumor suppressor, regulates the DNA damage response and apoptosis. Mutations in TP53 can lead to loss of function, impairing its ability to induce cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. The pathway involves genes like CDKN1A, GADD45, BAX, BAK1, DDB2, and POLK, all critical in DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell cycle control. Dysfunctional TP53 disrupts these processes, increasing genomic instability and tumorigenesis. This contributes to various cancers, most notably Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary condition with a high risk of multiple malignancies.  
\boxed{Li-Fraumeni syndrome}

The SOD1 allele, when mutated, contributes to **Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)**. The ERBB4 allele, specifically in the context of neuregulin (NRG) signaling, is involved in neuronal development, synaptic function, and myelination. The HTT allele, encoding the huntingtin protein, is associated with **Huntington's disease**. \boxed{Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3}

\boxed{Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4F}

The RET allele in this pathway contributes to the development of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), a hereditary cancer syndrome. RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that, when mutated, leads to constitutive activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, promoting cell proliferation and survival. These mutations are strongly associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, as well as pheochromocytoma and parathyroid adenomas. The activation of this pathway is a key driver in the oncogenic process.  
\boxed{Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2}

The PFN1 gene encodes profilin 1, a protein involved in actin dynamics. Mutations in PFN1 are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the progressive loss of motor neurons. These mutations disrupt normal actin filament assembly, leading to cytoskeletal dysfunction and neuronal degeneration. Thus, the PFN1 allele contributes to **amyotrophic lateral sclerosis**.  
\boxed{Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis}

The PSEN1 allele is involved in a genomic pathway leading to apoptosis, characterized by the activation of CASP3 and CASP7 through APAF1 and CASP9. PSEN1 and PSEN2 are key regulators of γ-secretase, which processes amyloid precursor protein (APP) into amyloid-β (Aβ). Accumulation of Aβ is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. This pathway also involves mitochondrial calcium dysregulation, leading to mitochondrial permeability transition (MPTP), release of cytochrome c, and subsequent apoptosis. These processes are implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Alzheimer's disease.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The PRKN gene encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Mutations in PRKN are a major cause of early-onset autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease (PD). Parkin plays a role in mitochondrial quality control and cellular stress responses. Disruption of its function leads to impaired mitochondrial function, increased oxidative stress, and neuronal degeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra, hallmark features of Parkinson's disease.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The HTT gene encodes the huntingtin protein, which is central to the genetic pathway defined. Mutations in HTT, particularly CAG trinucleotide repeat expansions, lead to the production of a toxic form of the huntingtin protein. This dysfunctional protein causes progressive neurodegeneration, primarily affecting the basal ganglia and cerebral cortex. The resulting disease is **Huntington's disease**, an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor dysfunction, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. The pathway elements, including CxIII and CytC, are involved in mitochondrial function and apoptosis, suggesting that HTT mutations disrupt mitochondrial integrity and neuronal survival.  
\boxed{Huntington's disease}

The RET allele, when mutated, activates the RET* proto-oncogene, initiating a signaling cascade through RAS (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS), RAF (BRAF, ARAF, RAF1), MEK (MAP2K1, MAP2K2), and ERK (MAPK1, MAPK3). This pathway is critical for cell growth and survival. RET mutations lead to constitutive activation of this pathway, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation and tumor formation. This contributes to medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC).  
\boxed{Medullary thyroid carcinoma}

The PIK3CA allele, as part of the PI3K-AKT-MTOR-S6K pathway, contributes to uncontrolled cell growth and survival by hyperactivating the pathway. This leads to increased proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, and metabolic reprogramming. Such dysregulation is strongly associated with various cancers, particularly breast, colon, and endometrial cancers.  
\boxed{Cancer}

The PRKN gene encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in mitochondrial quality control. Mutations in PRKN are a major cause of autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease (PD). The pathway involves ubiquitination processes, as indicated by genes like UBCH7/8 (E2 enzymes) and UBE2L3/6, which assist in ubiquitin conjugation. SNCA, encoding alpha-synuclein, is also implicated in PD pathology. Dysfunctional parkin leads to impaired mitophagy, accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and subsequent neuronal degeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons. This contributes to the progressive motor and cognitive deficits characteristic of Parkinson's disease.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The PINK1 allele is associated with **Parkinson's disease**. PINK1 (PTEN-induced kinase 1) is a serine/threonine kinase that plays a critical role in mitochondrial quality control by initiating mitophagy through the parkin (PRKN) pathway. Mutations in PINK1 lead to impaired mitochondrial function, increased oxidative stress, and neuronal degeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. The pathway involving PINK1, PRKN, and MFN1/2 is essential for maintaining mitochondrial integrity and function. Dysfunctional PINK1 activity contributes to the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor symptoms such as tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The PSEN1 allele is involved in a genomic pathway affecting amyloid-beta processing, as it regulates GSK3B, which modulates tau phosphorylation. This pathway also interacts with the KIF5+KLC complex, crucial for intracellular transport. Dysregulation of this network is implicated in Alzheimer's disease, characterized by amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. PSEN1 mutations are strongly associated with early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The PSEN1 allele is involved in the amyloidogenic pathway, which contributes to the production of amyloid-beta peptides. This pathway includes PSEN1, GSK3B, and the KIF5+KLC complex, which are associated with intracellular transport and processing of amyloid precursor protein (APP). Mutations in PSEN1 are strongly linked to early-onset Alzheimer's disease. The biological effect of this PSEN1 allele is the promotion of amyloid-beta accumulation, a hallmark of Alzheimer's pathology.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The PRKN allele is associated with **Parkinson's disease**. PRKN encodes parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase critical for mitochondrial quality control via the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Mutations in PRKN, particularly in autosomal recessive forms, lead to loss of parkin function, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction, increased oxidative stress, and neuronal degeneration, especially in dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra. This genetic defect is a major cause of early-onset Parkinson's disease.  
\boxed{Parkinson's disease}

The APP allele is central to the amyloidogenic pathway, leading to the production of amyloid-beta (Abeta) peptides. Accumulation of Abeta is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, contributing to neurotoxicity, synaptic dysfunction, and neurodegeneration. The pathway described involves Abeta-induced NMDA receptor activation, calcium influx, mitochondrial calcium overload via MCU, and eventual mitochondrial permeability transition, releasing cytochrome c and triggering apoptosis. These events are key mechanisms in Alzheimer's pathogenesis.  
\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The TPO allele in this pathway is critical for thyroid hormone synthesis. TPO catalyzes the oxidation and coupling of iodinated tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin (TG) to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT), and ultimately triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4). Mutations in the TPO gene impair this process, leading to congenital hypothyroidism. This condition results in inadequate thyroid hormone production, causing developmental and metabolic issues, particularly in neonates.  
\boxed{Congenital Hypothyroidism}

The NAGS allele, associated with the gene *NAGS* (N-acetylglutamate synthase), is involved in the urea cycle pathway. NAGS catalyzes the synthesis of N-acetylglutamate, a critical allosteric activator of CPS1 (carbamoyl-phosphate synthase 1), which is essential for ammonia detoxification. A deficiency in NAGS leads to a complete block in the urea cycle, resulting in hyperammonemia. This condition is known as **N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency**, a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The disease is characterized by neonatal-onset hyperammonemia, encephalopathy, and severe neurological damage if untreated. Early diagnosis and management with a low-protein diet and arginine supplementation can help mitigate symptoms.

\boxed{N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency}

The ATXN3 gene is associated with spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), a neurodegenerative disorder. ATXN3 encodes a protein involved in autophagy, and its dysfunction can lead to the accumulation of misfolded proteins. The provided pathway highlights ATXN3's interaction with autophagy-related genes (BECN1, PIK3C3, ATG14, PIK3R4, AMBRA1), underscoring its role in autophagic processes. Dysfunctional ATXN3 may impair autophagy, contributing to neuronal degeneration. This allele’s effect, therefore, is linked to SCA3.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3}

The BRAF allele in this genomic pathway is part of the MAPK/ERK signaling cascade, which regulates cell growth and survival. Mutations in BRAF, particularly the V600E mutation, dysregulate this pathway, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation. This pathway is commonly activated in cancers such as melanoma, thyroid cancer, and colorectal cancer. The BRAF* notation suggests a mutated or activated form of BRAF. Given its role in this pathway and the associated genes (MEK, ERK), this allele is strongly linked to **melanoma**.  
\boxed{Melanoma}

The SMO allele is part of the Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway, which regulates cell growth, differentiation, and organ patterning. Mutations in *SMO* can lead to constitutive activation of this pathway, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation. This dysregulation is implicated in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), a common type of skin cancer. Additionally, *SMO* mutations are associated with nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome), a hereditary condition marked by multiple BCCs and other developmental abnormalities. The pathway's interaction with GLI, SUFU, KIF7, and other regulators highlights its role in developmental and oncogenic processes.  
\boxed{Basal cell carcinoma}

The APP (amyloid beta precursor protein) allele contributes to **Alzheimer's disease**. The pathway described involves the cleavage of APP to produce Abeta, which accumulates and forms plaques, a hallmark of Alzheimer's. The downstream effect on CxIV (cytochrome c oxidase IV) and H2O suggests mitochondrial dysfunction, as cytochrome c oxidase is a key component of the electron transport chain. This mitochondrial impairment may exacerbate neuronal damage, contributing to cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.

\boxed{Alzheimer's disease}

The ERBB4 allele is part of a signaling pathway involving NRG genes, which are ligands for ERBB4, a receptor tyrosine kinase. This pathway is critical in neuronal development, synaptic function, and myelination. Mutations or dysregulation of ERBB4 have been implicated in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. Specifically, ERBB4 is associated with **schizophrenia**, as it plays a role in brain connectivity and neurotransmission. Variants in ERBB4 may disrupt normal neural circuitry, contributing to the pathophysiology of this disease.  

\boxed{schizophrenia}

The ATXN1 allele is associated with **Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1 (SCA1)**, a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive loss of coordination and motor function. ATXN1 encodes ataxin-1, a protein whose expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat leads to its toxic accumulation, disrupting normal cellular processes, particularly in Purkinje neurons of the cerebellum. This pathway involves interactions with RORA and KAT5, which modulate gene expression and epigenetic regulation, influencing downstream targets like ITPR1, SLC1A6, and GRM1—genes involved in calcium signaling, neurotransmitter transport, and glutamate receptor function. These disruptions contribute to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration observed in SCA1.  
\boxed{Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 1}

The CDKN2A allele encodes p16INK4a, a key inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK4/6), which regulates the G1/S transition in the cell cycle. Mutations or loss of CDKN2A function disrupt this regulation, leading to uncontrolled cell proliferation. This pathway also involves TP53, which, when activated, induces CDKN1A (p21) to halt the cell cycle. Inactivation of CDKN2A bypasses this checkpoint, contributing to tumor development. This pathway is frequently altered in melanoma, a type of skin cancer. Thus, CDKN2A mutations are strongly associated with melanoma risk. 

\boxed{Melanoma}
